title: 人工智能为研究人员指明了隐藏在线粒体中的新疾病靶点
content:
AI points researchers toward new disease targets hidden in mitochondria
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Artificial intelligence is helping Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists fast-track answers to a long-standing question in human biology: What do hundreds of mystery proteins in the mitochondria actually do?
For years, scientists have known that about 1,100 proteins exist within mitochondria, the energy centers of human cells, but they still don't know what many of them do.
This presents a problem because mutations in nearly 30% of mitochondrial proteins have been linked to human diseases, from more common conditions like cancer, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's to rare inherited metabolic disorders.
Pairing up proteins for answers
Without knowing the precise biochemical function of these proteins, it is difficult to understand the causes of these diseases. One way to infer a protein's function is to identify which other proteins it interacts with.
In the study "The predicted interactome of the human mitochondrial proteome," published in Nature Communications, the team used an AI tool to screen every possible pairing of about 1,100 human mitochondrial proteins—more than 630,000 combinations—for likely interactions. The predictions linked many disease-associated proteins to previously unknown biological pathways, pointing to potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets.
From a basic science perspective, the study also gave 85 previously uncharacterized proteins their first probable partners, offering clues about what those proteins may do in cells.
"If we don't know the function of these individual proteins, we cannot determine how to treat the diseases they may cause," said Abhinav Swaminathan, Ph.D., the study's lead author and an AgriLife Research scientist in the lab of Vishal Gohil, Ph.D., professor and Chancellor EDGES Fellow in the Texas A&M Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics.
Repurposing an AI tool that predicts protein shape
Researchers nationwide have been working to identify the functions of the mystery mitochondrial proteins to solve this problem, but traditional lab methods are slow.
Nearly three years ago, Swaminathan and Gohil set out to speed things up by testing an artificial intelligence tool called AlphaFold-Multimer, or AFM.
Google DeepMind created and unveiled AFM in 2022 to predict the three-dimensional shapes that proteins form together.
"We didn't have reliable experimental tools to evaluate direct mitochondrial protein interactions for the mitochondrial copper pathway proteins we study, so we ran a trial using the AI approach," Swaminathan said. "It worked really well, so we decided to apply it to all human mitochondrial proteins."
Out of the 630,003 possible protein pairs, the team cataloged 2,895 likely interactions. More than half of them had never been reported before.
Confirming AI predictions in the lab
About two years of laboratory experiments followed, confirming several of the predicted partnerships in yeast and human cells. Some of these experiments were performed in collaboration with researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.
The results showed AI predictions can serve as a road map, pointing scientists toward lab experiments most likely to yield results. The team made its predictions available as a free online resource, MitoMatch, so researchers worldwide can assign likely partners to the proteins they study.
As team members continue experimenting with the data, they are also collaborating with other researchers to better understand cell function and work toward new insights into human disease.
Cures for mitochondria-linked diseases may still be far into the future, but Swaminathan said the team's recent success with its AI approach is a promising starting point.
"We are a traditional biochemistry and genetics lab, not an AI lab," Swaminathan said, "but I think this research was successful because we asked the bigger question about what we could do to address the protein function problem, and we got creative with our resources to develop a solution that anyone can use."
Publication details
Abhinav B. Swaminathan et al., The predicted interactome of the human mitochondrial proteome, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77112-z
Journal information: Nature Communications
Provided by Texas A&M University

report.summary: AI预测线粒体蛋白互作组，挖掘出新的疾病靶点
report.background: 人类线粒体约含1100种蛋白，其中许多功能至今未知，而近30%的线粒体蛋白突变与癌症、帕金森、阿尔茨海默及罕见遗传代谢病相关。传统实验室鉴定蛋白功能耗时漫长。蛋白质的功能往往体现在它与谁结合，因此推断蛋白互作成为破题关键。DeepMind 2022年发布的AlphaFold-Multimer本用于预测蛋白复合物三维结构，得州农工大学团队将其“挪用”为大规模互作筛选工具，成果发表于Nature Communications。
key_points: 研究团队用AlphaFold-Multimer对约1100个线粒体蛋白的全部630,003种配对逐一打分，筛出2,895个高置信度互作，其中过半为此前从未报道的新发现。
85个此前功能完全未知的“孤儿”蛋白首次获得可能的结合伙伴，为推断它们在细胞中的角色提供了第一条线索。
许多与疾病相关的蛋白被连接到此前未知的生物学通路上，为诊断标志物和药物靶点提供了候选方向。
团队随后用约两年酵母与人类细胞实验验证了部分预测，证明AI结果可作为“实验路线图”，优先指引最可能成功的实验。
所有预测以免费在线资源MitoMatch开放，全球研究者可查询自己关注的蛋白的潜在伙伴。
值得注意的是，该团队自述是“传统生化遗传实验室而非AI实验室”，成功来自把大问题转化为可计算的问题。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，这是一次结构预测模型“二次利用”的范例：模型不只是预测形状，还能被改造成大规模假设生成引擎，说明生物基础模型的商业与科研价值在于下游任务编排。对开发者，门槛并不高——关键是把公开模型与领域数据、实验验证闭环结合。对普通用户，短期看不到直接产品，但罕见线粒体病的诊断与靶点发现有望提速，长期影响药物研发方向。
report.tools: 想跟进可关注AlphaFold-Multimer/AlphaFold3（结构预测）、MitoMatch（本研究开放的线粒体互作预测库）、STRING与BioGRID（蛋白互作数据库，可做交叉验证）、UniProt（蛋白功能注释），以及PyMOL或ChimeraX用于查看预测复合物结构。
